title: Restructuring, M&A & International Finance (CMA P2-B · feeds FAR/BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — MBG already runs an internal capital structure

MBG fact: MBG and Riverton are linked by an intercompany note (MBG note receivable 89012 ↔ Riverton note payable 89013), a real example of structuring capital between related entities. This week introduces the strategic-finance topics that sit on top of valuation: mergers and acquisitions, corporate restructuring, and international finance.

Mergers and acquisitions — motives and types

Firms combine to capture synergy — value the combined entity creates beyond the sum of the parts. Types: horizontal (same industry/stage — two general contractors), vertical (supplier or customer — a GC buying a framing sub), and conglomerate (unrelated). Motives include economies of scale, market access, vertical control, tax attributes, and diversification. Not all motives create value; "growth for growth's sake" and empire-building destroy it.

Synergy = value(combined) − [value(A) + value(B)]. Using an illustrative example: MBG standalone value $8,000,000, a target $4,000,000, combined value $13,500,000. Synergy = $13,500,000 − $12,000,000 = $1,500,000. The maximum MBG should pay for the target is its standalone value plus the synergy: $4,000,000 + $1,500,000 = $5,500,000. Paying more transfers all the created value to the seller.

Valuation and consideration

Targets are valued by discounted cash flow (intrinsic), comparable-company multiples, and precedent transactions. For a private target — like most construction firms — multiples and precedent deals carry the weight because there is no market price (the private-company limit from month 7). Consideration can be cash (clean, taxable to the seller, uses the acquirer's liquidity/debt capacity) or stock (shares risk and reward, may defer seller tax, dilutes the acquirer). A deal is accretive if it raises the acquirer's EPS and dilutive if it lowers it.

Corporate restructuring

Restructuring reshapes the asset or capital base: divestitures and spin-offs shed non-core units; recapitalization changes the debt/equity mix; debt restructuring renegotiates terms to relieve distress. For MBG the relevant version is internal: how capital is allocated between entities through the intercompany note and equity, and how those balances eliminate on consolidation (month 7, week 4). Sound intercompany structuring keeps each entity adequately capitalized for its own bonding.

International finance

Cross-border operations add foreign-exchange risk (transaction, translation, and economic — building on ASC 830 from month 7), country/political risk, and transfer-pricing considerations between affiliated entities in different jurisdictions. Firms manage FX exposure with natural hedges (matching foreign revenues and costs) and financial hedges (forwards, options). Transfer prices between related parties must reflect arm's-length pricing for tax compliance — the same intercompany discipline MBG applies to 89010/89011, scaled across borders.

Accretion, dilution, and the acquisition method

When a deal is paid in stock, whether it helps the acquirer's owners turns on a simple comparison the exam loves: a stock-for-stock acquisition is accretive when the acquirer's P/E is higher than the price-to-earnings multiple it pays for the target (so it "buys" cheaper earnings) and dilutive when it pays a higher multiple than its own. A high-multiple buyer acquiring a low-multiple target raises its own EPS purely from the multiple arbitrage; the reverse destroys EPS even if the businesses fit. Cash deals avoid share dilution but consume liquidity and debt capacity. Under the acquisition method (the consolidation accounting from FAR), the buyer records the target's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, and any excess of purchase price over net identifiable fair value becomes goodwill — an asset tested for impairment, not amortized. A bargain purchase (price below fair value) instead books a gain.

The three foreign-exchange exposures

International operations create three distinct exposures. Transaction exposure is the gain/loss on specific foreign-currency receivables and payables between booking and settlement (the worked euro-equipment loss from month 7, week 4). Translation (accounting) exposure is the effect of restating a foreign subsidiary's statements into the reporting currency — parked in OCI under the current-rate method. Economic (operating) exposure is the deepest: the change in the present value of future cash flows from long-run rate movements that shift competitiveness, even with no foreign-currency transactions on the books. Firms manage these with natural hedges (matching foreign revenues and costs), forwards and futures (lock a rate), options (insure against adverse moves while keeping upside), and currency swaps.

Transfer pricing and country risk

Between affiliated entities across borders, transfer prices must be set at arm's length for tax compliance; accepted methods include the comparable-uncontrolled-price, cost-plus, and resale-price methods. Aggressive transfer pricing to shift income to low-tax jurisdictions invites adjustment and penalties — the same integrity discipline MBG applies to its domestic intercompany accounts, scaled up. Cross-border deals also carry country/political risk (expropriation, capital controls, instability) that is layered into a higher discount rate or mitigated through insurance and financing structure. The recurring traps: confusing accretion with strategic fit (a deal can lift EPS yet destroy value, or create value yet dilute EPS), and ignoring economic exposure because no transaction is denominated in foreign currency.

Synergy types, due diligence, and a worked accretion

Synergies come in identifiable forms, and naming them disciplines the valuation. Revenue synergies (cross-selling, market access) are notoriously optimistic and are discounted heavily by experienced acquirers; cost synergies (eliminating duplicate overhead, purchasing scale) are more reliable; financial synergies (a stronger combined balance sheet, lower cost of capital, usable tax attributes) are real but bounded. Only synergies that are probable and quantifiable should drive the price — paying today for hoped-for revenue synergies is how acquirers overpay.

Due diligence is the safeguard: verifying the target's earnings quality, contingent liabilities, and customer concentration, and — for a contractor target — its WIP schedule, backlog, surety relationships, and the realism of its percentage-of-completion estimates. A target that has been pulling profit forward through aggressive estimates is worth far less than its reported earnings suggest.

A worked accretion check: MBG (illustratively) trades at a 12× price-to-earnings multiple and acquires a target for stock at an effective 9× the target's earnings. Because MBG issues shares worth 12× earnings to buy earnings priced at 9×, the deal adds more earning power per new share than it dilutes — it is accretive. Had it paid 15× for the same earnings, the new shares would carry less earning power than MBG's existing base and the deal would be dilutive, no matter how compelling the strategic story sounded. The number and the narrative must agree before a combination makes sense. For MBG, the same discipline that keeps its intercompany notes balanced to the penny is what should govern any acquisition price: pay for verified value, not for a persuasive story, and let the accretion math veto a deal the strategy slides cannot.

CPA Crossover — FAR / BAR

FAR tests business-combination accounting (acquisition method, goodwill, intercompany eliminations) and foreign-currency standards; BAR tests synergy, valuation multiples, and accretion/dilution. Expect a synergy or maximum-price computation and a question separating accretive from dilutive deals. The intercompany and FX threads here connect directly to month 7, week 4.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify a combination as horizontal, vertical, or conglomerate, and test whether it creates synergy.
  2. Compute synergy and the maximum price a buyer should pay.
  3. Choose cash versus stock consideration and judge accretion/dilution.
  4. Identify FX, country, and transfer-pricing risks in cross-border finance.

Recap: M&A is justified only by real synergy ($1,500,000 in the example, capping the price at $5,500,000); restructuring reshapes the asset and capital base; and international finance layers FX and transfer-pricing risk onto the same intercompany discipline MBG already practices.

flashcards.front: Horizontal vs vertical vs conglomerate merger
flashcards.back: Horizontal = same industry/stage; vertical = supplier/customer; conglomerate = unrelated.
Comparable-company multiples and precedent transactions (no market price for DCF cross-check).
Accretive raises the acquirer's EPS; dilutive lowers it.
Cash is clean and taxable to seller; stock shares risk/reward, may defer seller tax, dilutes acquirer.
Arm's-length pricing for tax compliance (same discipline as MBG's intercompany accounts).

questions.q: Standalone values are $8,000,000 and $4,000,000; combined value is $13,500,000. Synergy is:
Given $1,500,000 of synergy and a target standalone value of $4,000,000, the maximum a buyer should pay is:
questions.explain: Max price = target standalone + synergy = 4,000,000 + 1,500,000 = 5,500,000; paying more gives all value to the seller.

questions.q: A general contractor acquiring a framing subcontractor is a:
questions.explain: Acquiring a supplier in the production chain is a vertical merger.

questions.q: A private construction target has no market price. Which valuation approach carries the most weight?
questions.explain: Without a market price, multiples and precedent deals are used (the private-company limit).

questions.q: An acquisition that lowers the acquirer's earnings per share is:
questions.explain: A deal that reduces EPS is dilutive; one that raises EPS is accretive.

questions.q: Transfer prices between affiliated entities in different countries must:
choices: Be set as high as possible
Reflect arm's-length pricing for tax compliance
questions.explain: Related-party transfer prices must be arm's-length to satisfy tax rules across jurisdictions.

questions.q: Which is a corporate restructuring action rather than an acquisition?
questions.explain: A spin-off reshapes the existing asset base; the others are acquisition activities.
